---
title: "AI Detectors Are Reliable Enough to Be Dangerous"
description: "A profile of the AI-writing detector Pangram argues that a mostly-accurate detector deployed at scale is riskier than a broken one."
author: synesis
date: "2026-07-05"
image: cover.jpg
---

![AI-detection tools have become the first step in most public AI-writing accusations. Image from [The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/05/pangram-ai-detection-accuracy/687381/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/05/pangram-ai-detection-accuracy/687381/) profiles [Pangram](https://www.pangram.com/), the AI-writing detector behind most recent high-profile accusations, and argues that a detector accurate enough to trust but not accurate enough to be right is the more dangerous kind.

What the article reports:

- Pangram has become the de facto standard. It was behind [a horror novel pulled days before release](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/05/ai-writing-scandal-future-of-truth-book/687290/), accusations against articles in *The New York Times*, [prize-winning short stories](https://www.theatlantic.com/books/2026/05/granta-ai-fiction-book-scandal-changes-everything/687243/), and parts of [Pope Leo XIV's encyclical](https://x.com/linchzhang/status/2059755186810441935), and it is used by universities and scientific associations. It connects to [Canvas](https://www.instructure.com/canvas), so teachers can scan student submissions at scale.
- Pangram claims a false-positive rate near one in 10,000, and a University of Chicago analysis found almost no false positives on ~3,000 sample texts. But its false-negative rate is closer to one in 70, and "humanizer" tools like [Walter Writes AI](https://walterwrites.ai/) reliably flipped AI text to "human-written" in the author's tests.
- CEO [Max Spero](https://x.com/max_spero_) says Pangram should "never be the ending arbiter" but a starting point, and concedes the model's inner workings are "pretty uninterpretable." Its "AI-assisted" label spans everything from a grammar check to near-ghostwriting.
- Real accusations are already misfiring: a *Wall Street Journal* editor [called Pangram a "defamation machine,"](https://www.wsj.com/opinion/the-ai-detector-as-defamation-machine-8ba298f0) and Pangram itself later [found it had wrongly flagged](https://x.com/max_spero_/status/2055433575504249121) a Taylor Lorenz story. The piece compares the coming AI-detection wars to the 2023–24 plagiarism-detection accusations.

## My Notes

- **The base-rate problem**: with more than 30 million US students each turning in dozens of assignments, even a one-in-10,000 false-positive rate produces a steady stream of wrongful accusations. The problem is structural, and it is the one that survives every improvement to the model.

- **The "AI-assisted" label**: collapsing grammar-check, thesaurus use, brainstorming, and near-ghostwriting into a single category means the detector cannot draw the line that actually matters, and neither can the person acting on its verdict. That is an ontology problem no amount of calibration fixes.

- **Non-stationary accuracy**: the labs optimize for human-sounding output and humanizer tools exist specifically to defeat detectors, which makes [detecting AI text](/posts/20230120-chatgpt-human-expert-comparison/) an adversarial moving target. Any third-party audit is months old on arrival, so an institution citing a 95% accuracy figure is quoting a number that no longer describes the tool. This is the same theme as [celebrating human work](/posts/20260531-not-ai-generated/) rather than trying to certify its absence of AI.

- **The black-box accusation**: Pangram cannot say why it flagged a passage, so an appeal has nothing to contest. That is the same divide as [catching a lying LLM](/posts/20231008-catching-lying-llm/) with a black-box test versus one that can point inside the model, and it is why the plagiarism-detection comparison in the article is apt: those tools were also opaque, also trusted, and also wrong often enough to ruin people.
